speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have come to the end of Budget 2022 and the Committee of Supply (COS).

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, although we have been battling the pandemic for over two years, this is the first time that it reached the Chamber.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some Members of Parliament (MPs) were close contacts of those who were COVID-positive and took leave of absence out of an abundance of caution even.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Special seating arrangements were put in place, so they could feel at ease about still attending.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A number of MPs, myself included, contracted COVID-19 and had to sit out of the proceedings for a while.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Members of the Ruling Party had it; Ms Sylvia Lim, Ms He Ting Ru from Workers' Party got it; Prof Hoon, a Nominated Member of Parliament got it as well.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But I would like to thank colleagues for their care and concern and expressions of support for all those who were ill.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He did add as an afterthought that he was concerned for my health as well.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is the highest level of participation in the last five years despite the reduced number of Members of Parliament able to attend Parliament.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, this Budget was developed against the backdrop of climate change and climate risk which is becoming more urgent by the day.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Third, just as we were about to debate the Budget, the world changed with the situation in Ukraine, reminding us once again that independence, the right to self-determination and territorial sovereignty are precious and should never be taken for granted, and why small countries like Singapore must continue to advocate and uphold an international order that is rules based and principled.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With this Budget, we will be strengthening our business ecosystem and building stronger Singaporean enterprises.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The "Singapore Global Enterprises" and the "Singapore Global Executive Programme" will help us produce companies and Singaporean talent that are globally competitive.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Budget 2022 will also revitalise and support our F&B, retail and tourism sectors.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will continue to press on with our digitalisation journey, while ensuring those less comfortable with technology are not be sidelined.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This Budget affirms our support for our workers, especially low-wage workers.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This unique approach is the outcome of intensive effort between the Tripartite partners: the Labour movement, employers and Government.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As this is not without trade-offs and costs, Singaporeans will be engaged in this endeavour so that we can all have a clear understanding of what it will take to achieve our green ambitions even as we move forward on them.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have renewed and strengthened our social compact.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Cost of living, inflation are very much on people's minds.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Almost all Members spoke on this in one way or another.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Approving the Household Support Package and other help schemes paves the way for us to help Singaporeans through this tough period.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We heard assurance from the Minister for Finance during his round-up speech that the Government would "not hesitate to take further actions to protect jobs, and to help households and businesses deal with increased costs, if need be." We have ensured we can meet and pay for the healthcare needs of our rapidly ageing population.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are redoubling our efforts to bridge inequality and make sure no one is left behind.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: ComLink will be scaled up nationwide and UPLIFT expanded.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There will be more opportunities for the differently abled.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We reaffirmed the importance of family – 2022 will be the year of celebrating families and strengthening support for families.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: All these good things cannot come to pass without funding.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To enable them to happen, we enhanced and strengthened our tax structure.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will adjust the corporate tax system to take into account BEPS.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We increased the progressivity of our personal income tax.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We raised wealth taxes through targeted increases in property tax and tax on luxury cars.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And we increased GST with a significant package to buffer its impact and adjusted the timing.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will study further support if the inflation situation worsens.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And in Parliament, the Budget process saw robust debate.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The value of robust debate is that it helps to crystalise the issues and it lets people see where Members of Parliament and Parties stand.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And I thought it might be helpful here if I just summarise the difference in approach between the Government and the Opposition, in particular, the Workers' Party, not to reignite the whole debate on this again.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But just to summarise what the different philosophical approaches are, so that people can look at it and make their own judgements and determination.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Everyone contributes, but those who have more, contribute more.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Those with less also contribute but a lesser amount and receive more in return.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Keeping the tax burden manageable for all, including businesses so that there is incentive for all to work hard, do well and enjoy the benefits of their hard work even as they contribute to our revenues.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We still maintain the protection of our reserves and we use the income on our reserves equitably – 50% for this generation, 50% for the next.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Workers' Party has a different philosophical approach.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They have preferred not not to raise GST.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But I do not think there is any dispute that there is a genuine and real need though to fund healthcare, going forward and that there is a need for increased revenue.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: No matter which way you cut it, it boils down to those three things: tax companies more, tax the rich more, or use more of the reserves.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And even if we are able to collect more in corporate taxes from the revenues from BEPS 2.0, we will have to use these revenues for additional measures to enhance our overall competitiveness and ensure that we can continue to attract our fair share of investments.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On taxing the rich, there are ramifications on whether we will drive away talent and wealth, and that will be bad for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Using more of the reserves means leaving less behind for the next generation and imposing higher taxes on them.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, I just lay this out at the end of the day, so that people can reflect, make their own conclusions and see how they wish to view this.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But I thought when all was said and done, and the dust settled after the debate, it is good just to crystallise the two different positions, so that people will have a more meaningful insight as to what the different propositions actually mean.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Next, with more Opposition Members in Parliament, it is natural that our debates will get more robust.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, in this session, we are also reminded that whilst robust debate is good, it is also important that Members maintain decorum in their actions, both in and outside of the House.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Standing Orders are there for a reason.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Timelines and deadlines are also there for a reason – to enable us to conduct parliamentary business efficiently but also effectively.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I, therefore, urge Members to be mindful of this, so that for future debates, we can have all the cut and thrust that we desire but, at the same time, observing all due proprieties.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It has been a tiring but rewarding two weeks.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Budget was the product of strong input from Singaporeans from all walks of life; we engaged widely, took in feedback.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It reflects our citizens' needs, aspirations and does its best to address their concerns.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I would also like to express my gratitude to all of the public servants who have been working so hard on this, on top of their regular work.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Many have had to learn on the job, some have taken on additional "COVID-fighting" roles over the past two years or so and then have had to deal with Budget.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It has been a tiring time for them but they soldier on, because when they signed up for Public Service, they knew they also signed up to serve, even at personal cost in terms of family time and rest.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I would also like to thank the Deputy Leader for covering for me in my absence.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On behalf of the House, I would like to thank you, Mr Speaker, and your deputies for presiding over the proceedings with patience and forbearance.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are also grateful to the Clerk of Parliament, the Parliament Secretariat, the staff, the interpreters and translators, all of whom have been working in overdrive these last few weeks.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Actually, there were more Budgets if you count the multiple Budgets that we had in 2020.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But as a wrap-up speech, this is my fifth one.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Every year, the night before, or two nights before, barely any sleep because you are trying to distil the last one and a half to two weeks’ worth of discussions, discourse, and all the work done into a “Too Long Didn’t Read” (TLDR) version.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: People often say, “Government communications cannot make it!

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Why can’t you keep it simple?” I can tell you that Government is trying.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But the reality is this: when you are in the business of making things work, when you are in the business of actually having to do the real work and the heavy lifting, the details do matter.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is very different when you have to carry them out.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I remember a few years ago, when Chee Meng was Minister for Education, and I, as a parent, as all of us as parents would have a lot of issues about MOE, said “Eh, why is your MOE policy like that?”.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Then, I remember Chee Meng replied to me, “Why don’t we switch jobs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Suddenly, everything took on a very different hue.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is easy to critique and it is important for us to critique.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But when we actually have to bear the responsibility of translating those ideas, views and opinions into reality, it looks very, very different.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, in the same way, I would say that it is very difficult to distil everything down into a meme or a TikTok clip.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And I would not be able to do that.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As we all know, are we able to satisfy every need and want?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Many of you here who work, you have your own organisation, whether you are the leader of your political party or your company, school – we know that we are not always able to do that.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Budget and COS process is very involved.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This year, we had blue and yellow featuring, red and white, and of course, green!

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I do not know whether Minister Grace Fu is wearing green today.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: She had been wearing green almost every day.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And it can get quite technical as well.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am not going to repeat all that.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am not going to "BEPS" you until you "COMPASS", or "TRECS" you with "JOY" or "HEIDI".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But what I will do is to take a step back.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have been going through all the details, the technical and all the different things that are required in the Budget to make things happen.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And really three main themes: the world we live in, the worries and uncertainties that we are grappling with now; the post-truth world that we live in; and the world that we live in in terms of the bigger stories, noting that all of us zoom into the individual stories that we share.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is important, sometimes, to be able to also zoom out and look at the bigger picture and the bigger story.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We certainly live in worrying and uncertain times.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We are still in the grips of COVID-19 although, increasingly, we are learning to live with it.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This was a recurrent theme that many of you have raised.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have been jittery for some time because we are living in a fast-changing world.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We are living amid a Fourth Industrial Revolution.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We are concerned about things changing as our children go to school and universities, and by the time they graduate, is the world going to move on, is it going to be relevant?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Will we lose our verve as an economy?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And with that longevity, lower birth rates, the burden on healthcare costs?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And we worry also about the climate and how is it going to change and affect us, and especially our children’s generation?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But if there is any consolation, it is affecting everyone on Earth.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We are not spared; we are not the only ones; everyone is grappling with these issues.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The world we live in is also – and many of you would be familiar with this term – a Post-Truth World, whatever that definition might be.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But essentially, these days, truth might seem indeterminant, malleable.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Or is truth determined by “Well, this is what I believe, what I feel, what I hear”, and therefore it becomes the “truth”?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Is it based on whoever says it loudest?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Whoever says it more passionately, eloquently, or more coolly?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But that is the world we live in.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Many of us zoom in and share stories about how individuals are affected.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We use stories to illustrate gaps and concerns so that we can have better policies to help.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But some use stories to indict, to remonstrate.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But we all know that stories can be false.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Stories can also be used out of context.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And the question for us as leaders and Parliamentarians is, what do we do with these stories?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: On the ground, we know how these examples could manifest itself.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: For example, in my area in Chai Chee, we have rental flats.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You can go to a rental flat and some of you who are involved in the work will realise when you come to a flat, it is messy, a lot of stuff that is there.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And you feel, how on earth can Singaporeans live in such abject poverty in First World Singapore?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But if you step next door, in the same one-room rental flat, the neighbour, it is clean, tidy.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In fact, some of my residents take great pride in explaining to me how they go to Daiso and decorate their house quite nicely with whatever they buy from Daiso.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You are impressed by their resilience, by their ingenuity.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We talk about the metaverse, but this is almost like a multi-verse that we live in.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Same, similar facts, stories, but then we walk away with very different impressions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do we then not ask, where is the family in the overall scheme of things?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And the Government has a role to play.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But this is how stories can manifest themselves in many, many different ways.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We are living in a world where we have more information than ever before.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In fact, information is increasing at exponential rates.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We are, like I said earlier, the TLDR generation.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If it takes a few more swipes left or right, up or down, it just takes too much time, it is just too tedious.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have so much information we don’t know how to process it.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have so much to distract us: Netflix, Minecraft, K-Drama, and some of you have been playing Wordle or Quordle, which is even worse!

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Many of us are better educated, more critically minded.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But if we ask ourselves honestly, how many of us actually read?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And because we are kind of smart and we have opinions and views about things, do we formulate those opinions very quickly?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Or are we just too busy with all the different things distracting us?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We go to certain commentators for their distillation of the issues of the day rather than just reading it ourselves.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have “live” broadcast of Parliament today, but how many of us actually go to the source and actually listen to what was said?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Or do we listen to what is being said by others?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You can lament all you want, you can describe it, but that is the reality.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Iswaran shared from Ernest Hemingway’s “The Sun Also Rises”.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am less cultured than he is, so I can only share from a book that I find quite telling, “Factfulness” by Hans Rosling.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: While some might criticise Rosling for being overly positive, my main takeaway is that, as human beings, our nature, are we sometimes not really very evidence-based?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have this instinct to be negative, “Oh, the world is a lot worse than it is today”.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We tend to blame, we like to generalise and so on.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It distorts the way we look at things.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But there are real-life implications to how all these things play themselves out.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The important question for all of us as leaders in this Parliament, in this environment, is to realise that this playbook, sadly, actually works.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Which is why you see many politicians using it.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The rise of the far-right or even the far-left are examples of that.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do we play fast and loose with the stories we use?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do we just lift “facts” from chat groups, or wherever it might be?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do we use anecdotes recounted to us without checking whether it is true?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Or is it a case of what I believe is true and therefore, it is?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Also, in this world where we are all politically correct, are we just too shy, too scared to take a stand, lest we be accused of being closed-minded, being cancelled out on social media?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This is a reality of the world – it is not going to go away.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think it is just going to get worse, if you will.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But the important question both for us as Members of Parliament and Singaporeans at large is what do we do with that?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And especially for us in this Chamber, how do we then carry out our roles?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do we exploit these gaps and these trends?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: When that erodes, we have no basis to lead.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Often, the negativity and misinformation serve to do one thing.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do we end up being no different from any Internet forum?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: That is something all of us need to decide.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We need to ask ourselves, is it creeping into our own political discourse?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The last point I would like to end on is the bigger story, the world we live in.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We zoom into all these individual stories and like I said, they are important, but as leaders, we must also have the ability to zoom out and sometimes remind ourselves of the larger trends.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But we sometimes forget all the different things that are happening around us.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And a very big “Thank You” to every single one of you who has made this possible.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I also want to take the opportunity to thank our public officers who continue to serve to the best of their ability, despite the challenging times.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Many of them, apart from creating policies, are also at the frontlines because they need to double up, because there are other responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Dr Tan Yia Swam, Dr Wan Rizal and Dr Janil have talked about being understanding to our healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think it is worth reminding us to bear in mind to treat all our public officers with decency and respect.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There will be those who fall afoul of what we would expect of them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But for the vast majority of them, they are doing their best to look after all of us.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It behooves us to at least accord them that basic dignity and respect.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I remember during the debate on public housing a few days ago, I was quite struck by it.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We were discussing about waiting times for HDB flats, eligibility ages, about housing in prime locations, about EIP concerns.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Of course, there are areas to improve and there are concerns that we need to assuage.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But I am also reminded by my many residents who come to me to tell me that they are going off, some of them getting married, forming new families, they email me, they message me.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: At a wake two nights ago, a senior executive shared – at first, it would seem he was griping that the sandwiched class is not getting anything and only the lower-income gets – that he works in the aviation industry and he was quite candid, that without the Government grants and assistance, he might have lost his job.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Many more of his colleagues might have lost their jobs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And in many indirect ways, he has benefited too.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Many of my residents share the same, whether they are running big businesses, small businesses, many of them having jobs in management positions, they are glad that the policies that all of you have created have helped.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Real income has moved, especially at the lower income level.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: With all the different steps taken, with Progressive Wage, with Workfare, it will continue to go up.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You have seen the projections in terms of where those wages will go.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: From a healthcare perspective, I think a lot of us will have views about how the COVID-19 situation should be run.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But I guess the question we should ask ourselves is, “If we were in the position of the MTF, what would we do?”.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: When we have to balance life and livelihood, would it be quite so simple?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The truth is, as you take a step back, you see we have a strong trust among our people, a strong trust between our people and our healthcare authorities, which allowed us to be able to carry out our safe management measures (SMMs); which allowed us to be able to be vaccinated; which had enabled us to keep deaths low and serious illnesses at bay, by and large, and enabled us to move on to the next stage, to deal with the concerns that we have.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Schools remained open, students continued to be educated.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: On the social front, despite all the challenges, we look at the contributions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In 2020, it went up to $16.1 million.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Slight dip in 2021 but $15 million still.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Giving.sg, $93.4 million in 2020, $95.6 million in 2021.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Lawrence Wong was asked, amid all the concerns with cost and inflation and so on, what would we do.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will just end off on this point.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is that we are in good health.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The policies that we have taken are not easy.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The easiest path to take for any government of the day is to spend and keep your electorate happy.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: In my view, it is completely politically naïve to talk about balanced Budget, to talk about tax increases when you have reserves.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I do not know what the reserves comprise.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And GIC, I am not even going to ask Minister Lawrence what the amount is, but we keep it confidential for strategic reasons.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But we do have a fair bit of reserves.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And we have seen how that came into play in the last few years.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Should the situation arise in the coming years, I have no doubt that MOF would step in and do what needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But we are only able to do that because we are healthy.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And that is the only powder that we have.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Which is why a Budget like this is important.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As we deal with the present, we also need to deal with the future.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As we deal with the individual needs, we also need to step back and look at the bigger picture.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But all these can only be done when you have the support of the people.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And in Parliament, as we debate this, it is important that we communicate as effectively as we can, win the hearts and minds.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We are not going to be able to convince everyone.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Not everyone will feel that they benefit equally.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But on balance, are we able to uplift lives?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are we able to make things better for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And to look after our people well today, and for tomorrow.
